faqs.a: JSON-LD (JavaScript Object Notation for Linked Data) is Google's recommended format for structured data: a <script type="application/ld+json"> block in your page. Alternatives are Microdata and RDFa, but JSON-LD keeps the markup separate from your visible HTML, which is cleaner and less error-prone.

Yes — valid structured data is required for rich results like FAQ dropdowns, star ratings, and recipe cards in search. But validity alone doesn't guarantee them; Google decides when to show rich results based on relevance and quality too.
faqs.q: Does valid schema improve my search results?

faqs.a: Copy the <script type="application/ld+json"> block from your page source (View Source, not the rendered page) and paste the JSON inside the script tags — or paste the whole script block; the parser reads the JSON content.
faqs.q: How do I get the JSON-LD from my page?

faqs.a: An error means a required field is missing or the structure is broken — fix these first, they can disqualify the markup. A warning means a recommended field is missing — the markup still works, but adding it improves eligibility for rich results.
faqs.q: What is the difference between an error and a warning?

faqs.a: Use @graph when one page needs several top-level entities (for example a WebPage plus a BreadcrumbList plus an FAQPage). This validator reads @graph arrays and checks each block separately.

This tool checks structure and required fields against schema.org shapes. Google's Rich Results Test additionally checks Google-specific policies (like which types earn which rich results). Use both: this one for fast iteration, Google's for final confirmation.

schema-markup-validator.formula:
Validation rules per block:
1. @context must exist and reference schema.org.
2. @type must exist; if it is one of the 20 known types, its required fields are checked.
3. Required field missing or empty -> error.
4. Recommended field missing -> warning.
Checked types: Article, BlogPosting, NewsArticle, Product, FAQPage, Recipe, Event, Organization, LocalBusiness, WebSite, WebPage, BreadcrumbList, Review, Person, JobPosting, SoftwareApplication, VideoObject, HowTo, ItemList.
howTo: Copy the JSON-LD from your page (the content of the <script type="application/ld+json"> block).
Paste it into the box above. @graph arrays and plain arrays are handled automatically.
Read the totals: blocks found, errors, and warnings.
Fix every error — missing required fields can disqualify the markup from rich results.
Add recommended fields flagged as warnings, then re-paste to confirm a clean result.
keyFacts: Structured data (schema.org vocabulary) helps search engines understand your page content and can unlock rich results.
JSON-LD is Google's recommended format: a script block separate from your visible HTML.
Every block needs @context (usually https://schema.org) and @type (like FAQPage or Product).
Each type has required properties — for example FAQPage needs mainEntity, Product needs name, Article needs headline.
Missing recommended properties (author, image, datePublished) won't break the markup but weaken rich-result eligibility.
Invalid or incomplete markup simply earns no rich result — there is no penalty, just a missed opportunity.
schema-markup-validator.keywords: schema markup validator, json-ld validator, structured data checker, schema.org validator

labels.eMissingField: Required field "{v}" is missing or empty.
labels.eNoType: @type is missing — every block needs a schema.org type.
labels.emptyState: Paste your JSON-LD above to validate it against schema.org shapes.
labels.noIssues: No issues found — this block looks valid.
labels.parseError: This is not valid JSON. Check for trailing commas, missing quotes, or truncated content.
labels.wUnknownType: "{v}" is not in the known type list — required fields were not checked.

limitations: Checks structure and fields, not Google's rich-result policies — passing here doesn't guarantee a rich result.
Only 20 common types have required-field rules; unknown types get a warning instead of a full check.
Cannot verify that URLs, dates, or nested entities inside the markup are correct.
Does not fetch your live page — it validates exactly the JSON you paste.

schema-markup-validator.workedExample:
Sample input — an FAQPage block:
{
  "@context": "https://schema.org",
  "@type": "FAQPage",
  "mainEntity": [
    {"@type": "Question", "name": "What is X?", "acceptedAnswer": {"@type": "Answer", "text": "X is…"}},
    {"@type": "Question", "name": "How does Y work?", "acceptedAnswer": {"@type": "Answer", "text": "Y works by…"}}
  ]
}
Checks traced by the tool:
1. Blocks found: 1.
2. @context references schema.org: ok.
3. @type FAQPage is a known type: ok.
4. Required field mainEntity present and non-empty: ok.
5. Recommended fields for FAQPage: none defined — no warnings.
Result: 1 block, 0 errors, 0 warnings — valid markup.
